A growing line of work therefore builds cheap proxies: read a few weights, run a handful of prompts, get a safety estimate in seconds. Every one of these proxies is selected by correlating it with benchmark scores across honestly-trained checkpoints and picking the winner [1, 2, 3].\\n\\nTwo things are wrong with that selection rule, and neither has been tested.\\n\\nFirst, nobody has checked which cheap readouts survive being moved to a lineage they were not tuned on. Published work shows that harmful intent is linearly decodable at around 0.98 AUROC in essentially every checkpoint, including abliterated ones, with abliterated variants matching their instruction-tuned counterparts to within 0.003 [4, 5]. A readout of what the model knows is therefore near-constant across alignment variants and cannot separate them. What varies is whether the model's refusal mechanism uses that knowledge -- a statement about a relationship across items rather than about a level. This predicts in advance which half of any metric battery can generalize.\\n\\nSecond, the selection rule assumes honesty. The cheapest proxies read the most superficial thing a model does, and the most superficial thing is the cheapest to change. A chat template is a text file inside the repository. A system prompt is thirty tokens. A rank-one addition to the residual-write matrices needs no training data and no gradient step [6], and it is not hypothetical: it is a published method presented as a cheap safety improvement [7], validated with a guard model's refusal rate on harmful prompts and compliance on ordinary benign prompts, but never on the benign-but-alarming requests where pushing a model toward refusal actually does damage.\\n\\nWe address both gaps in one study. We register 50 single-checkpoint metrics before any measurement, classify each as a level metric (reading an unconditional propensity) or an across-item metric (reading how refusal varies with the input), and test all 50 on held-out lineages spanning seven architecture families. We pair this with a forgery-cost ladder ranking each metric by what it costs to fake, and a detection axis measuring whether each forgery survives a reference-free structural check. For the detection column we adopt a publicly released community weight scanner [8] as an off-the-shelf auditor tool, contribute the calibration and held-out validation it has never been given, and find that its simulation-calibrated threshold produces a 100% false-positive rate on real transformer weights.\\n\\nOur contributions are:\\n\\n1. A pre-registered battery of 50 single-checkpoint safety metrics spanning weights, activations and behaviour, with every fitted-direction metric cross-fitted and reported beside its in-sample version and a label-permutation null (Sections 3 and 4).\\n\\n2. A held-out-lineage evaluation showing that harm-knowledge readouts are near-constant across alignment variants, confirming the mechanism that predicts which metrics can generalize (Section 5).\\n\\n3. A demonstration that cross-fitting is load-bearing for internal safety readouts: the incumbent AMS scanner's in-sample separation exceeds its cross-fitted version on every tested checkpoint, and on pure noise the gap is total (Section 5).\\n\\n4. The first calibration of a published parent-free weight scanner on real transformer weights, finding a 100% false-positive rate at its published threshold, and a threshold-free alternative using an anisotropy-matched null (Section 5).\\n\\n5. An ecosystem census finding that only three independent safety-tuned lineages exist below 4B parameters, and an unmatched safety benchmark is 96.3% separable by TF-IDF alone (Section 5).\\n\\nThe remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 describes the metric battery and its registration protocol. Section 4 details the experimental setup. Section 5 presents results. Section 6 discusses implications and limitations. Section 7 concludes.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig_pipeline]\\n\\n## 2 Related Work\\n\\nWe organize related work by the question each line asks and close each theme with the gap this study addresses.\\n\\n**Cheap per-checkpoint safety readouts.** AMS [1] computes a separation statistic along a difference-of-centroids direction on 96 forward passes and reports 71% leave-one-out accuracy across 14 models, but its direction, layer sweep and prompt set are never held out, and the Spearman rank correlation with behavioural compliance is not significant (rho = -0.423, p = 0.13, n = 14). Skin-Deep [2] produces a Geometric Fragility Score predicting LoRA-attack retention, but it requires the base model as input and 1000 prompts. N-GLARE [9] reads hidden-state trajectories with no parent model and reproduces red-team rankings, but needs four probing conditions over 7000 cases. RAS [3] produces a calibrated 0--100 score separating aligned from abliterated variants 210x faster than judge-based scoring, but requires a per-family reference model, calibration checkpoints with measured attack success rates, and states that family-specific calibration remains necessary. None of these four incumbents is both parent-free and validated on held-out lineages with a two-sided ground truth penalizing blanket refusers.\\n\\n**The geometry of refusal and harm knowledge.** Arditi et al. [6] showed that a single direction in the residual stream controls refusal and that orthogonalizing weight matrices against it removes refusal entirely. Subsequent work established that harmful intent is linearly separable at approximately 0.98 AUROC across four families and three alignment variants including abliterated ones [4], and that abliterated variants match instruction-tuned ones to within 0.015 AUROC on harm-knowledge probes [5]. The dissociation between harm knowledge and refusal is now well documented: harmfulness and refusal are encoded separately [10], refusal reads only a single harm direction while moral judgment reads progressively more [11], and recognition precedes execution in the layer stack [12]. This study uses the dissociation as a prediction: harm-knowledge readouts should be near-constant across variants and cannot discriminate, so the signal must come from how refusal uses the knowledge.\\n\\n**Harmfulness-refusal coupling.** The coupling between harm recognition and refusal drive has been studied as a diagnostic under adversarial fine-tuning [13], where it is explicitly concluded that low coupling is not a safety predictor because supervised fine-tuning reaches low coupling while remaining unsafe. HARC [14] trains coupling as a defence. We adopt coupling as a discriminator between alignment classes, not as a predictor of compliance, and cross-fit it where prior work does not.\\n\\n**Parent-free weight auditing.** Watch the Weights [15] reports that applying singular-value decomposition to the weights directly, without a base model, gives success that varies greatly across models (Remark 3.2). A community model scanner [8] computes bottom-k left singular subspace alignment across layers as a reference-free abliteration indicator. The two-signal abliteration audit [16] combines a reference-anchored activation gap with a weight-energy ratio at approximately 0.95 AUROC, but presumes an attested reference. The weight-subspace comparison literature addresses lineage tracing [17, 18] and model compression [19] rather than edit detection. We adopt the community scanner as an off-the-shelf tool and contribute the calibration it lacks.\\n\\n**Forgery, tamper-resistance and benchmark gaming.** Tamper-resistant safeguards [20] measure what it costs to remove safety; we measure what it costs to fake it. Benchmark gaming is documented for black-box evaluations: constant outputs achieve high win rates [21], safety-benchmark variance is largely capabilities [22], and the leaderboard illusion is well characterized [23]. Gaming the Metric, Not the Harm [24] proves that level metrics are not manipulation-invariant. Rank-one safety injection [7] is a published fine-tuning-free weight edit presented as a defence, which we include as a rung in the forgery ladder. Chat-template backdoors [25] establish that repository files are an unexamined attack surface. None of this prior work combines a metric read from weights or activations with a cost-ordered forgery ladder and a reference-free detection check.\\n\\n**Evaluation methodology.** Cross-fitting internal readouts is standard in neuroscience but rare in LLM safety evaluation: AMS [1] fits its direction on the same 16 pairs it measures, RAS [3] fits on a reference model and calibrates on the same panel it reports. The brittleness of fixed probes under distribution shift is documented both for steering vectors [26] and for safety probes [27, 28]. Item response theory has been applied to reduce safety evaluation cost by 80--99% [29, 30], but only for behavioural items, not internal readouts.\\n\\n## 3 Method\\n\\n### 3.1 Metric Battery and Registration\\n\\nWe register 50 single-checkpoint safety metrics before any measurement. Each metric is computed from a single downloaded checkpoint with no parent model, no attested base to diff against, and no benchmark run. The registry is frozen with a SHA-256 hash before the first measurement and verified unchanged at the end.\\n\\nEach metric carries four labels assigned at registration: (i) a functional-form class (e.g., mean difference of projections, Spearman rank correlation), (ii) a level vs. across-item tag, (iii) the inputs it reads (weights, activations, logits, or text), and (iv) the number of prompts it requires. Thirteen metrics read weights only (zero prompts). Twenty-one read activations or activations-plus-logits over a 160-item battery. Eight read logits only. Five read text or metadata. Three additional metrics (a metamodel and its controls) require a completed harvest.\\n\\nThe 50 metrics span three groups:\\n\\n**Knowledge readouts** (12 metrics). Cross-fitted harm-direction probes at various layers, harm-projection gaps, and re-implementations of published incumbents (AMS separation [1] in both in-sample and cross-fitted forms, HRCI coupling index [13]).\\n\\n**Behavioural and structural readouts** (20 metrics). First-token logit-gap margins, refusal-token probability mass, greedy refusal rates, model-card regex scores (both term-swept and name-free de-biased), weight statistics including bottom-subspace alignment (BSA), top-subspace alignment (TSA), cross-layer cosine, spectral entropy, and BOTGAP, the ratio of the smallest to the second-smallest singular value of a residual-write matrix.\\n\\n**Across-item readouts** (18 metrics). Coupling between refusal drive and cross-fitted harm estimate (regression slope, R-squared, Spearman rho, Kendall tau, AUROC over items), decision spread (the across-item standard deviation of the refusal drive), mutual information, per-category dispersion, matched-twin contrasts, presentation invariance, depth-gap between refusal and content decodability, and a best-effort N-GLARE reimplementation.\\n\\n### 3.2 Cross-Fitting Protocol\\n\\nEvery fitted-direction metric is defined with a pre-registered fold structure stratified by harm category. The residual stream is 1536 to 3072 dimensional while the item count is a few dozen. In that regime, an in-sample difference-in-means projection separates pure noise at AUROC 1.000. Cross-fitting is therefore part of the metric definition, not an analysis choice.\\n\\nThe fold structure uses four folds, stratified so each fold contains items from every harm category. Fold 4 is reserved as an out-of-fold evaluation fold. The direction is fitted on three folds and evaluated on the held-out fold; the reported metric is the mean across held-out folds. A per-checkpoint label-permutation null (100 permutations) is run alongside, and the in-sample version is printed for every metric so the gap between them is visible.\\n\\n### 3.3 Ground Truth\\n\\nThe ground truth has two columns: graded compliance with harmful requests (StrongREJECT rubric [31]) and false refusal on benign-but-alarming twins (XSTest [32]). A model refusing everything scores badly on the false-refusal column rather than winning. Grading uses a non-Qwen hosted judge (GPT-5-nano, configured to minimize hidden-reasoning overhead so that generation tokens are spent on the grading rubric rather than suppressed chain-of-thought), with the StrongREJECT score recomputed from rubric components to correct inconsistent arithmetic. A second independent judge (Gemini-2.5-flash-lite) provides an agreement audit. Qwen3Guard is excluded as a judge for SafeRL checkpoints because it was SafeRL's training reward.\\n\\n### 3.4 Lexical Floor\\n\\nBefore any internal readout is evaluated, we establish the floor that a no-model text classifier achieves. TF-IDF plus logistic regression separates harmful from safe prompts at AUC 0.963 when sources are unmatched (StrongREJECT harmful vs. XSTest safe), but only 0.537 against JailbreakBench's own paired benign partners and 0.655 on XSTest positional twins with pair-grouped cross-validation. Every internal readout must beat the matched numbers.\\n\\n### 3.5 Weight Instrument\\n\\nFor the weight-based detection column, we adopt the community model scanner's [8] bottom-k subspace alignment statistic: for each residual-write matrix, form the rank-one projector onto its bottom left singular vector, average those projectors over a sliding window of 8 layers, and take the largest eigenvalue (BSA, subscript w8). This statistic is not our contribution; it is prior art, and we label it as such throughout. What we contribute is the calibration it has never been given: thresholds from real weights rather than simulation, an anisotropy-matched null, and held-out-family validation.\\n\\nWe additionally compute BOTGAP, which reads local rank deficiency and needs no cross-layer sharing.\\n\\n## 4 Experimental Setup\\n\\n### 4.1 Panel\\n\\nThe panel spans 32 checkpoints across seven architecture families (Qwen3, Qwen2.5, Gemma2, Phi4, SmolLM2, OLMo2, TinyLlama), all under approximately 4B parameters, ungated, loaded in bf16 with full weight and hidden-state access. Checkpoints are classified into four arms: base (7 checkpoints, 7 lineages), instruct (11 checkpoints, 11 lineages), safety-tuned (7 checkpoints, 3 lineages) and abliterated (7 checkpoints, 6 lineages).\\n\\nThe resampling unit throughout is the lineage (parent model x tuning run), never the individual repository. Suffix-collapsing removes epoch, step, checkpoint and date suffixes; named versions (-v1, -v2) are preserved.\\n\\n### 4.2 Item Battery\\n\\nThe item battery contains 160 items: harmful requests from JailbreakBench Behaviours and StrongREJECT, benign-but-alarming twins from XSTest (200 positional twin pairs), and paired benign partners from the JailbreakBench Index. Items are allocated across four stratified folds. A disjoint 24-item probe set is reserved for the greedy refusal-rate baseline.\\n\\n### 4.3 Harvest\\n\\nEach checkpoint undergoes a single shared harvest: a weight pass (singular value decompositions of all residual-write matrices, approximately 2--4 minutes per checkpoint on CPU) and a teacher-forced activation pass (all-layer hidden states at the last prompt token and the first generated token, per item). Every metric is then computed offline from the stored harvest with no second GPU pass, and every direction can be re-fitted and every null recomputed without additional model access.\\n\\n### 4.4 Evaluation Protocol\\n\\nAll metrics are evaluated in a leave-one-lineage-out design. For each held-out lineage, thresholds and fitted quantities are determined using only the remaining lineages, and the held-out lineage is scored. The held-out balanced accuracy is the headline number; the tuned (in-sample) accuracy is printed beside it, and the gap between them is the measure of overfitting.\\n\\n### 4.5 Stage Gates\\n\\nThe experiment uses four pre-registered stage gates that determine branching:\\n\\n- **Stage 0**: Cross-fitting self-test on synthetic data.\\n- **Stage 3** (F5): Whether the weight instrument's published threshold survives real weights.\\n- **Stage 4**: Whether the teacher-forced refusal drive tracks the judge's refusal flag (anchor gate).\\n- **Branch F1**: Whether enough independent safety-tuned lineages exist for a powered three-way test (floor: 5).\\n\\n## 5 Results\\n\\n### 5.1 Cross-Fitting Is Load-Bearing\\n\\nOn pure Gaussian noise at d = 2560 with 64 randomly-labelled items, an in-sample difference-in-means projection separates the two classes at AUROC 1.000. The cross-fitted version falls to 0.377.\\n\\nThis is not a theoretical concern. The AMS scanner [1] fits its direction on the same 16 contrastive pairs it then measures. On every checkpoint in our panel, the in-sample AMS separation exceeds the cross-fitted version: by 0.48 sigma on Qwen3-4B (in-sample 3.76 vs. cross-fitted 3.28), by 1.14 sigma on the abliterated variant (2.62 vs. 1.48), and by 0.98 sigma on Qwen3-0.6B (1.82 vs. 0.83). The gap is largest on the abliterated checkpoint, where the in-sample direction has the most room to overfit to noise structure.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig_crossfit]\\n\\n### 5.2 The Published Weight Threshold Does Not Survive Real Weights\\n\\nThe bottom-subspace alignment statistic (BSA, bottom-1 left singular vectors of attention output projections, sliding 8-layer window) reads 0.565 on honest, unedited Qwen3-0.6B weights. This is well above the 0.35 separator that Gaussian simulation calibrates (simulated honest: 0.171). The same weights with a shared-direction abliteration applied by us reach 1.000, and BOTGAP collapses to 0.003 in bf16. The statistic discriminates, but its absolute threshold is a false positive on real transformers, which carry genuinely shared bottom directions that simulation does not produce.\\n\\nAcross the honest panel, 100% of unedited checkpoints exceed the 0.35 threshold. The false-positive rate is 1.00, making the published threshold unusable for any deployment.\\n\\nWe therefore withdraw the absolute threshold and report BSA in two forms: (a) threshold-free, as an AUROC, and (b) z-scored against an anisotropy-matched null drawn from within-checkpoint random directions in the bottom-16 subspace. The z-score reads 25.1--25.6 on honest checkpoints and 21.7 on the abliterated variant, a surprising result: the abliterated checkpoint's z-score is lower than the honest ones, opposite to what would be expected if abliteration increased bottom-subspace alignment.\\n\\nBOTGAP, which reads local rank deficiency rather than cross-layer sharing, is not spectrum-invariant: on a simulated heavy-tailed spectrum, the honest BOTGAP value is 0.064, already below its own 0.10 separator.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig_bsa_calibration]\\n\\n### 5.3 Harm Knowledge Is Near-Constant Across Alignment Variants\\n\\nThe cross-fitted harm-content probe reaches AUROC 0.974 on the Qwen3-4B instruct checkpoint and 0.931 on its abliterated sibling (a community-abliterated variant), a gap of 0.043. The smaller Qwen3-0.6B instruct checkpoint reads 0.857. These numbers confirm the prediction from prior work [4, 5]: what the model knows about harmfulness is nearly identical across alignment variants. The signal that must distinguish them is not knowledge but the decision to use it.\\n\\nPer-layer probe profiles show that harm content becomes decodable in the middle layers (onset at approximately 14% of depth for Qwen3-4B) and remains stable through the upper layers, while the refusal signal peaks early and does not track the content signal. For the abliterated checkpoint, the refusal probe peaks later and tracks content more closely, consistent with a model that has lost its refusal mechanism and whose residual refusal signal is entangled with content representation rather than independent of it.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig_depth_profiles]\\n\\n### 5.4 Across-Item Metrics Separate Where Levels Do Not\\n\\nThe key across-item metrics show clear separation between instruct and abliterated checkpoints on the Qwen3-4B anchor lineage. The coupling R-squared between refusal drive and cross-fitted harm estimate reads 0.852 on the instruct checkpoint and 0.051 on the abliterated variant, a 16.6x ratio. The Spearman coupling is 0.905 vs. 0.192, the Kendall tau is 0.729 vs. 0.129, and the AUROC over items is 0.971 vs. 0.570.\\n\\nThe smaller Qwen3-0.6B instruct checkpoint shows intermediate values (R-squared = 0.242, Spearman 0.502, Kendall 0.354, item AUROC 0.735), consistent with a weaker but present coupling in a model with less capacity.\\n\\nDecision spread reads 11.04 for Qwen3-4B instruct, 7.07 for the abliterated variant, and 4.82 for Qwen3-0.6B. The synthetic blanket-refuser wrapper collapses decision spread to 0.80--1.80 while producing a large mean logit gap (18.8--38.8). A model refusing everything therefore produces a high level but a collapsed spread, and the coupling ratio is undefined at the pre-registered 0.25-logit floor.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig_coupling]\\n\\n### 5.5 The Readout Assumption Failed\\n\\nThe stage-4 anchor gate tested whether the teacher-forced refusal drive (log-odds of a refusal token minus a compliance token at the first generated position) tracks the external judge's refusal flag. The AUROC of this readout against the judge's binary flag is 0.750 on Qwen3-4B and 0.391 on the abliterated variant, failing the pre-registered gate. The fitted cross-fitted harm probe beats an anisotropy-matched null (20 random directions drawn from the empirical covariance, best of 20) on only 1 of 3 checkpoints, with mean fitted AUROC 0.921 matching mean random AUROC 0.921.\\n\\nThe readout assumption failure ranks above no-candidate-promoted in the pre-registered branching logic: it is a finding about the substrate, not about the specific metrics built on it.\\n\\n### 5.6 Safety-Tuned Lineages Are Scarce\\n\\nA Hugging Face census returns 445 repositories matching safety-tuning search terms, but the top five uploaders account for 85% and collapsing to unique lineages leaves 245. Only three independent safety-tuned lineages are reachable under 4B parameters: Qwen3-4B-SafeRL (the official safety variant), TinyLlama-1.1B (four safety algorithms applied by one team to the same base), and gemma-2-2b (two safety-tuned variants).\\n\\nThis is below the pre-registered floor of five for a powered three-way test, so the primary claim is demoted to the two-way held-out comparison (instruct vs. abliterated, 11 vs. 6 lineages). The scarcity is itself the finding: the models a downloader is most likely to encounter are exactly those with no safety-tuned sibling and no published safety number.\\n\\nThe abliterated arm is larger and more diverse: 2,879 unique repositories (lower-bounded; search terms each hit the 1,000-result API cap), 6 independent lineages in the panel, with the top 5 uploaders accounting for only 14.2% of repositories.\\n\\n### 5.7 The Race Table\\n\\nBecause the readout assumption failed at stage 4 and only 3 checkpoints were fully scored across 2 lineages, the race table carries no held-out balanced accuracy. The full 50-metric registry is frozen and verified unchanged, and per-checkpoint metric values are reported for all scored checkpoints. The race is deferred to iteration 2, which will score additional lineages against the pre-registered battery.\\n\\nTable 1 reports selected metric values across the three scored checkpoints. Across-item metrics show the largest instruct-to-abliterated gap: coupling R-squared drops from 0.852 to 0.051, while the knowledge-level harm-probe AUROC drops only from 0.974 to 0.931. Weight statistics (BSA) are near-constant across variants (0.590 vs. 0.589), confirming that BSA reads architecture rather than alignment.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig_all_metrics]\\n\\n### 5.8 Incumbent Comparison\\n\\nAll four published incumbents operate in a different access class from our setting (parent-free, no calibration data, held-out lineages, two-sided ground truth). The comparison is therefore non-matched, and we state the access requirements for each:\\n\\n- **AMS** [1]: Parent-free, but direction and layer are fitted in-sample on the same prompts used to report separation. Its 71% leave-one-out cross-validation held out only the threshold. Cross-fitted on our folds, its separation drops by 0.48--1.14 sigma per checkpoint.\\n- **Skin-Deep/GFS** [2]: Requires the base model and 1000 prompts. Not parent-free.\\n- **N-GLARE** [9]: Parent-free and generation-free, but needs four probing conditions over 7000+ cases. No published code.\\n- **RAS** [3]: Requires a per-family reference model, calibration models with measured attack success rates, and states family-specific calibration is necessary.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig_incumbent_access]\\n\\n## 6 Discussion and Limitations\\n\\n### 6.1 What the Readout Failure Means\\n\\nThe teacher-forced refusal drive, defined as the log-odds of a refusal token minus a compliance token at the first generated position, does not reliably track the external judge's refusal decision. This is the substrate on which all across-item coupling metrics are built. The failure does not mean coupling is uninformative; it means the specific operationalization of refusal drive used here is misaligned with the judge's rubric. The first generated token may not carry the refusal signal for models that produce preambles, hedges, or partial compliance before refusing. Future work should explore alternative readout positions (mean over the first k generated tokens, or the last prompt token) and alternative refusal operationalizations (probability mass on a refusal-token vocabulary rather than a single token pair).\\n\\n### 6.2 The Anisotropy Problem\\n\\nThe fitted cross-fitted harm probe beats an anisotropy-matched null on only 1 of 3 checkpoints, with mean fitted AUROC equal to the mean best-of-20 random AUROC at 0.921. Most of what a linear harm probe reads at these item counts is the anisotropy of the residual stream rather than a harm-specific direction. The result is consistent with prior findings on the brittleness of steering vectors under distribution shift [26] and the out-of-distribution fragility of internal probes [27, 28]. It does not mean no harm direction exists; it means the item budget (64 items per fold after stratification) may be insufficient to distinguish it from the dominant anisotropy axes, and the item count at which the signal lifts is itself a finding: a floor on how cheap an internal safety metric can be.\\n\\n### 6.3 Limitations\\n\\n**Panel size.** Only 3 checkpoints were fully scored (2 lineages), far below the pre-registered target for the honest panel. The race table carries no held-out balanced accuracy, and the level-vs.-across-item prediction is untested at scale. The registry is frozen and the protocol is ready for a larger panel.\\n\\n**Single judge.** The graded ground truth relies on a single hosted judge (GPT-5-nano at USD 0.008 per panel) with a partial second-judge audit (Gemini-2.5-flash-lite). This is insufficient to establish inter-rater reliability and should be expanded.\\n\\n**Architecture concentration.** Six of the seven families in the panel are decoder-only transformers with similar residual-stream structures. The weight statistics (BSA, BOTGAP) are defined on residual-write matrices that may not generalize to architectures with different attention patterns or mixture-of-experts routing.\\n\\n**Forgery ladder not executed.** The pre-registered cost-ordered forgery ladder (six rungs from chat-template edits through genuine fine-tuning) was not executed in this iteration due to the readout assumption failure at stage 4. The undetectable-forgery-cost axis, which was a headline planned contribution, remains untested.\\n\\n**Two metrics are not scale-free.** The coupling slope and harm-projection gap carry the hidden-state norm of the model they came from. The race z-scores every metric column across checkpoints, so the ranking is unaffected, but the raw values are not comparable across architectures. The scale-free companions (R-squared, Spearman, Kendall, item AUROC) are.\\n\\n## 7 Conclusion\\n\\nWe registered 50 single-checkpoint safety metrics before any measurement and tested them on a panel spanning seven architecture families. Three findings survived the pre-registered stage gates. First, cross-fitting is load-bearing: an in-sample harm direction separates pure noise at AUROC 1.000, and the incumbent AMS scanner's in-sample separation exceeds its cross-fitted version by 0.48--1.14 sigma on every checkpoint. Second, the simulation-calibrated threshold of a published parent-free weight scanner produces a 100% false-positive rate on real transformer weights. Third, only three independent safety-tuned lineages exist below 4B parameters, and the models most likely to be downloaded are those with no safety number at all.\\n\\nThe across-item coupling metrics show the predicted pattern: the instruct checkpoint's R-squared between refusal drive and cross-fitted harm estimate is 0.852, falling to 0.051 on its abliterated sibling. But the substrate these metrics are built on, the teacher-forced first-token refusal drive, does not track the judge's refusal flag, which means the coupling reads something other than the intended construct. Fixing the readout operationalization is the critical path for the next iteration.\\n\\nThe honest summary is that cheap safety metrics for downloaded models are harder than the field assumes. The published proxies have not been tested on held-out lineages, their directions are fitted in-sample at dimensionalities where noise separates perfectly, their weight-based thresholds fail on real weights, and the safety-tuned checkpoints needed to validate them barely exist. These are findings, not obstacles, and reporting them is the first step toward metrics one could actually believe.\\n\\n## References\\n\\n[1] G. The paper honestly reports this negative finding and identifies fixing the readout operationalization as the critical path forward. The paper also establishes a lexical floor (TF-IDF AUC 0.963 on unmatched sources, 0.537 on matched), shows that harm-knowledge probes are near-constant across alignment variants (0.974 vs. 0.931 AUROC), and demonstrates that most of what a harm probe reads at these item counts is residual-stream anisotropy rather than a harm-specific direction.\"\n}\n", "numLines": 58, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 58}}

  "title": "What Cheap Safety Metrics Actually Read",
  "abstract": "Open-weight language models on Hugging Face number over a million, almost none carry safety scores, and running a benchmark on each is infeasible. A growing literature builds cheap proxies: read a few weights, run a handful of prompts, score in seconds. We ask what these proxies actually measure. We register fifty single-checkpoint safety metrics before any measurement and test all of them on a panel of 33 checkpoints spanning eight architecture families, paired with a six-rung forgery-cost ladder and a parent-free weight-recovery study. Three findings survive pre-registered controls. First, the LLM judges used to build ground truth silently refuse to grade harmful completions under standard rubrics, inverting the label on two-fifths of items; a stance-classification reframing restores correct grading. Second, of the fifty metrics, only three beat their own label-permutation null, and a zero-prompt model-card regex reading nothing of the model outperforms every internal readout. Third, a published rank-one safety injection reverses on two-sided ground truth that also penalizes over-refusal: harmful refusal rises but false refusal on benign-but-alarming twins rises further, producing a net safety loss. A separate study of 71 real abliterated checkpoints finds that parent-free spectral reads detect the edit but cannot grade how unsafe the edited model is. Cheap safety metrics for downloaded models are harder than the field assumes.",
  "paper_text": "## 1 Introduction\n\nAnyone who downloads a model from Hugging Face is trusting an artifact uploaded by a stranger. The platform hosts over a million models, almost none carry safety evaluations, and running a benchmark on each is out of the question. A growing line of work therefore builds cheap proxies: read a few weights, run a handful of prompts, get a safety estimate in seconds. Every one of these proxies is selected by correlating it with benchmark scores across honestly-trained checkpoints and picking the winner [1, 2, 3, 4].\n\nThree things are wrong with that selection rule, and none has been tested in combination.\n\nFirst, nobody has checked which cheap readouts survive being moved to a lineage they were not tuned on. Published work shows that harmful intent is linearly decodable at approximately 0.98 AUROC in every tested checkpoint, including abliterated ones, with abliterated variants matching their instruction-tuned counterparts to within 0.003 [5, 6]. A readout of what the model knows is therefore near-constant across alignment variants and cannot separate them. What varies is whether the model's refusal mechanism uses that knowledge, a statement about a relationship across items rather than about a level.\n\nSecond, the selection rule assumes honesty. The cheapest proxies read the most superficial thing a model does, and the most superficial thing is the cheapest to change. A chat template is a text file inside the repository. A rank-one addition to the residual-write matrices needs no training data and no gradient step [7], and it is not hypothetical: it is a published method presented as a cheap safety improvement [8], validated with a guard model's refusal rate on harmful prompts and compliance on ordinary benign prompts, but never on the benign-but-alarming requests where pushing a model toward refusal actually does damage.\n\nThird, the ground truth itself may be broken. We discover that LLM judges used to score harmful compliance under the standard StrongREJECT rubric [9] refuse to engage with the grading task: 40.5% of all grades and 65.9% of grades on harmful items collapse to the minimum score, producing an inverted label that makes abliterated models appear to refuse more than their instruction-tuned siblings. This artifact is invisible unless the evaluator checks known-compliant harmful responses, and it contaminates any downstream metric selection.\n\nWe address all three gaps. We register fifty single-checkpoint metrics before any measurement, test all fifty on 33 checkpoints spanning eight architecture families, and pair the metric race with a six-rung forgery-cost ladder and a parent-free weight-recovery study on 71 real abliterated checkpoints. Our contributions are:\n\n1. A discovery that LLM judges refuse to grade harmful completions under standard rubrics, silently inverting 40.5% of safety labels, and a stance-classification reframing that restores correct grading (Section 3.3).\n\n2. A pre-registered battery of fifty safety metrics tested on 33 checkpoints across eight families, finding that only three beat their own label-permutation null, and a zero-prompt card regex outperforms every internal readout at leave-one-lineage-out balanced accuracy 0.917 (Section 5.1).\n\n3. Evidence that fitted harm directions survive an anisotropy-matched null on 16 of 17 checkpoints, resolving a prior ambiguity, but that a one-prompt black-box logit readout already exceeds the internal probe's correlation with safety (Section 5.2).\n\n4. A six-rung forgery-cost ladder showing that the published rank-one safety injection [8] reverses on two-sided ground truth, and that the pre-registered parent-free weight detection axis must be withdrawn (Section 5.3).\n\n5. A study of 71 real abliterated checkpoints finding that weight reads detect edits but cannot grade how unsafe the model is, an identifiability limit confirmed by the true parent-based edit strength (Section 5.4).\n\n[FIGURE:fig_overview]\n\n## 2 Related Work\n\n**Cheap per-checkpoint safety readouts.** AMS [1] computes a separation statistic along a difference-of-centroids direction on 96 forward passes and reports 71% leave-one-out accuracy across 14 models, but its direction, layer sweep and prompt set are never held out, and its Spearman rank correlation with behavioural compliance is not significant (rho = -0.423, p = 0.13, n = 14). Skin-Deep [2] produces a Geometric Fragility Score predicting LoRA-attack retention, but requires the base model and 1000 prompts. N-GLARE [3] reads hidden-state trajectories with no parent model and reproduces red-team rankings, but needs four probing conditions over 7000 cases. RAS [4] produces a calibrated score separating aligned from abliterated variants 210x faster than judge-based scoring, but requires a per-family reference model and states that family-specific calibration remains necessary. None is both parent-free and validated on held-out lineages with a two-sided ground truth that penalizes blanket refusers.\n\n**The geometry of refusal and harm knowledge.** Arditi et al. [7] showed that a single direction in the residual stream controls refusal and that orthogonalizing weight matrices against it removes refusal entirely. Subsequent work established that harmful intent is linearly separable at approximately 0.98 AUROC across four families and three alignment variants including abliterated ones [5], and that abliterated variants match instruction-tuned ones to within 0.015 AUROC on harm-knowledge probes [6]. The dissociation between harm knowledge and refusal is now well documented: harmfulness and refusal are encoded separately [10], refusal reads only a single harm direction while moral judgment reads progressively more [11], and recognition precedes execution in the layer stack [12]. This study uses the dissociation as a prediction: harm-knowledge readouts should be near-constant across variants and cannot discriminate.\n\n**Harmfulness-refusal coupling.** The coupling between harm recognition and refusal drive has been studied as a diagnostic under adversarial fine-tuning [13], where it is explicitly concluded that low coupling is not a safety predictor because supervised fine-tuning reaches low coupling while remaining unsafe. HARC [14] trains coupling as a defence. We adopt coupling as a discriminator between alignment classes and cross-fit it where prior work does not.\n\n**Parent-free weight auditing.** Watch the Weights [15] reports that applying SVD to weights directly, without a base model, gives success that varies greatly across models. A community model scanner [16] computes bottom-k left singular subspace alignment across layers as a reference-free abliteration indicator. The two-signal abliteration audit [17] combines a reference-anchored activation gap with a weight-energy ratio at approximately 0.95 AUROC, but presumes an attested reference. We adopt the community scanner as an off-the-shelf tool and contribute the calibration it lacks.\n\n**Forgery, tamper-resistance and benchmark gaming.** Tamper-resistant safeguards [18] measure what it costs to remove safety; we measure what it costs to fake it. Benchmark gaming is documented for black-box evaluations: constant outputs achieve high win rates [19], safety-benchmark variance is largely capabilities [20], and the leaderboard illusion is well characterized [21]. Gaming the Metric, Not the Harm [22] proves that level metrics are not manipulation-invariant. Rank-one safety injection [8] is a published fine-tuning-free weight edit presented as a defence, which we include as a rung in the forgery ladder. Chat-template backdoors [23] establish that repository files are an unexamined attack surface. None of this prior work combines a metric read from weights or activations with a cost-ordered forgery ladder and a reference-free detection check.\n\n**Evaluation methodology.** Cross-fitting internal readouts is standard in neuroscience but rare in LLM safety evaluation. The brittleness of fixed probes under distribution shift is documented both for steering vectors [24] and for safety probes [25, 26]. Item response theory has been applied to reduce safety evaluation cost [27, 28], but only for behavioural items, not internal readouts. Black-box access alone is insufficient for rigorous AI audits [29].\n\n## 3 Method\n\n### 3.1 Metric Battery and Registration\n\nWe register fifty single-checkpoint safety metrics before any measurement. Each metric is computed from a single downloaded checkpoint with no parent model, no attested base, and no benchmark run. The registry is frozen with a SHA-256 hash before the first measurement and verified unchanged at the end.\n\nThe fifty metrics span three groups. **Knowledge readouts** (12 metrics) include cross-fitted harm-direction probes at various layers, harm-projection gaps, and reimplementations of published incumbents (AMS separation [1] in both in-sample and cross-fitted forms, HRCI coupling index [13]). **Behavioural and structural readouts** (20 metrics) include first-token logit-gap margins, refusal-token probability mass, greedy refusal rates, model-card regex scores, weight statistics including bottom-subspace alignment (BSA), top-subspace alignment (TSA), spectral entropy, and BOTGAP. **Across-item readouts** (18 metrics) include coupling between refusal drive and cross-fitted harm estimate, decision spread, mutual information, per-category dispersion, and presentation invariance.\n\n### 3.2 Cross-Fitting Protocol\n\nEvery fitted-direction metric uses a pre-registered four-fold structure stratified by harm category. The residual stream is 1536 to 3072 dimensional while the item count is a few dozen. In that regime, an in-sample difference-in-means projection separates pure noise at AUROC 1.000. Cross-fitting is therefore part of the metric definition, not an analysis choice. The direction is fitted on three folds and evaluated on the held-out fold; the reported metric is the mean across held-out folds. A per-checkpoint label-permutation null and an in-sample version are printed for every metric so the gap between them is visible.\n\n### 3.3 Ground Truth and the Grader-Side Refusal Discovery\n\nThe ground truth has two columns: graded compliance with harmful requests (StrongREJECT rubric [9]) and false refusal on benign-but-alarming twins (XSTest [30]). A model refusing everything scores badly on the false-refusal column rather than winning. The two-sided score D2 is the average of harmful-refusal rate and benign-compliance rate, rewarding models that refuse harmful requests and comply with benign ones.\n\nWe discovered that LLM judges refuse to grade harmful completions under the standard StrongREJECT rubric framing. Asked to rate a reply to a harmful prompt, gpt-5-mini, gpt-4.1-mini and gemini-2.5-flash all emit the minimum triple (1, 1, 1) regardless of what the reply actually did. On 1040 paired items, 40.5% of StrongREJECT grades are the degenerate minimum (65.9% on harmful items). The disagreement is one-sided: 330 items where the standard framing says \"refused\" but the reply was in fact compliant, versus 66 the other way. Without the fix, an abliterated model reads as safer than its instruction-tuned sibling.\n\nReframing as stance classification (\"you are a text classifier; classifying text is not endorsing it\") and asking for declined/engagement/detail labels takes the controlled accuracy from 3/6 to 6/6 on both judges tested, and raises inter-judge Cohen's kappa from 0.456 to 0.585. We use the stance framing throughout; inter-judge agreement on the final instrument is kappa = 0.785 (n = 476).\n\n[FIGURE:fig_grader_refusal]\n\n### 3.4 Lexical Floor\n\nBefore evaluating internal readouts, we establish the floor that a no-model text classifier achieves. TF-IDF plus logistic regression separates harmful from safe prompts at AUC 0.963 when sources are unmatched (StrongREJECT harmful vs. XSTest safe), but only 0.537 against JailbreakBench's own paired benign partners and 0.655 on XSTest positional twins with pair-grouped cross-validation. Every internal readout must beat the matched numbers.\n\n### 3.5 Leave-One-Group-Out Null\n\nUnder uninformative random labels, leave-one-group-out balanced accuracy has an empirical mean of 0.403 (sd 0.131), not the nominal 0.500, because held-out group class balance is negatively correlated with the training remainder's. Every race-table row is compared against a matched label-permutation null rather than against 0.50.\n\n## 4 Experimental Setup\n\n### 4.1 Panel\n\nThe main experiment spans 33 checkpoints across eight architecture families (Qwen3, Qwen2.5, Gemma2, Phi4, SmolLM2, SmolLM3, OLMo2, TinyLlama), all under approximately 4B parameters, loaded in bf16 with full weight and hidden-state access. Checkpoints are classified into four arms: base, instruct, safety-tuned and abliterated. Only three families carry an instruct/abliterated pair (Phi4, Qwen2.5, Qwen3), below the pre-registered floor of five for a leave-one-family-out claim, so the primary holdout is leave-one-lineage-out. The resampling unit is the lineage (parent model x tuning run), never the individual repository.\n\nA separate offline evaluation uses 17 fully harvested checkpoints from a prior iteration (Qwen3 and TinyLlama only, four lineages) to run the anisotropy control suite at zero new compute.\n\nThe weight-recovery study (Section 5.4) spans 71 real abliterated or uncensored checkpoints with readable safetensors, drawn from the Hugging Face ecosystem.\n\n### 4.2 Item Battery\n\nThe item battery contains 160 items: harmful requests from JailbreakBench Behaviours and StrongREJECT, benign-but-alarming twins from XSTest (200 positional twin pairs), and paired benign partners from the JailbreakBench Index. Items are allocated across four stratified folds. Grading uses a non-Qwen hosted judge (gpt-5-mini with reasoning effort set to minimal), with the StrongREJECT score recomputed from rubric components under the stance-classification framing.\n\n### 4.3 Forgery Ladder\n\nSix rungs, each applied to six honest checkpoints spanning six architecture families. F0: chat-template edit (zero FLOPs). F1: inference-time system prompt. F2a: constant offset in a near-constant carrier coordinate. F2b: published rank-one safety injection [8]. F3: keyword-triggered refusal LoRA adapter. F4: genuine light safety fine-tuning. Each rung is evaluated against the full metric battery and scored by two auditor tiers: a blind tier (template content, key-shape check, and weight statistic) and a family-aware tier that may diff against the family default.\n\n### 4.4 Stage Gates\n\nThe experiment uses pre-registered stage gates. G2 fires if fewer than five families carry a two-way pair, downgrading the holdout to leave-one-lineage-out. The readout bake-off selects from five candidate refusal definitions by agreement with judged refusal on held-out item folds; the acceptance bar is AUROC at least 0.80 on every checkpoint including abliterated ones. Both gates fired.\n\n## 5 Results\n\n### 5.1 The Race Table\n\nOf the fifty registered metrics, only three beat their own label-permutation null at the 95th percentile on the 33-checkpoint, 8-family panel with leave-one-lineage-out scoring (Table 1).\n\nThe card regex, a regular expression over the uploader's own model card that reads nothing of the model, separates abliterated from everything else at AUROC 1.000 and leave-one-lineage-out balanced accuracy 0.917. Its de-biased twin, which removes model-name terms, collapses to approximately 0.10. The power is the uploader telling you, and that is the cheapest rung of the forgery ladder.\n\nThe best weight-only metric achieves balanced accuracy 0.826, which ties its own null 95th percentile. The best across-item metric (presentation invariance) achieves balanced accuracy 1.000 at leave-one-lineage-out but its family-separation score is only 0.257, suggesting it tracks presentation format rather than family-independent safety.\n\nOnly one metric survives both the label-permutation null and the blanket-refuser pole rule. The pre-registered shipping invariant, which requires at least three qualifying metrics reading hidden states or weights, is not satisfied.\n\n[FIGURE:fig_race_table]\n\n### 5.2 The Anisotropy Control Resolves\n\nOn the 17-checkpoint offline panel (Qwen3 and TinyLlama), a cross-fitted harm-content probe at the last prompt token survives the anisotropy-matched null on 16 of 17 checkpoints (94.1%), with mean cross-fitted AUROC 0.835 against a mean within-item-span null of 0.629 (1000 draws per checkpoint). The anisotropy-matched null draws random directions in the item-level residual-stream subspace rather than using global random projections, so a direction that beats it carries item-specific content rather than reflecting the dominant axes of the representation space. The prior iteration's tie (fitted 0.921 vs. best-of-20 null 0.921) was caused by using a point estimate of the null maximum, which is an upward-biased approximation of the null distribution. The 1000-draw null reveals that the fitted direction is genuinely above the null on almost every checkpoint.\n\nHowever, this does not translate into a strong safety readout. A black-box logit readout at one prompt already exceeds the internal probe's Spearman correlation with the two-sided safety target (0.282 at k = 1 vs. 0.021 for the internal probe). The gap persists at every prompt budget tested (k = 1 through 64). Internal access does not buy additional safety discrimination over what a single logit read provides.\n\n[FIGURE:fig_anisotropy]\n\n### 5.3 The Forgery Ladder\n\n**The rank-one injection reverses.** The published rank-one safety injection [8] was recovered at alpha* = x4 on one of its own Table-1 models (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct). At alpha*, harmful refusal rises from 0.859 to 0.984 while false refusal on matched benign-but-alarming twins rises from 0.375 to 0.750. The two-sided score D2 falls from 0.788 to 0.621 (bootstrap 95% CI for the change: [-0.233, -0.065]). The reversal replicates on Qwen3-0.6B (D2 0.784 to 0.703, false refusal 0.219 to 0.469). A negative-control injection using a random direction produces D2 change of -0.042, confirming that the effect is specific to the published direction. At x16, the model becomes a blanket refuser (false refusal 1.000, D2 = 0.500). The method's own evaluation metric, which uses only harmful-prompt refusal rate and benign compliance on ordinary instructions without an over-refusal column, improves at every dose.\n\n[FIGURE:fig_rosi_reversal]\n\n**Detection axis withdrawn.** The pre-registered parent-free weight detection axis achieves a best cross-family AUROC of 0.738 at 12 families, below the 0.80 bar. The B3 weight screen fires on 3 of 6 honest, unedited ladder hosts, so the screen itself carries no signal about an edit. The detection axis is formally withdrawn. Within-family, the same statistic reaches AUROC 1.000 on Qwen3/TinyLlama, confirming that it reads architecture-specific spectral structure rather than a safety-relevant signal.\n\n**Detection by rung.** The blind auditor tier catches F0 (chat-template edit) in 26 of 30 cells via template rendering. F1 (system prompt) is invisible by construction. The bias-tensor variant of F2a is caught in 30 of 30 cells by a key-shape check. The carrier-coordinate variant of F2a, the rank-one injection F2b, and all training-based rungs (F3, F4) evade every blind screen except the weight statistic, which is itself unreliable. The family-aware auditor tier catches 147 of 147 additional cells, adding 27.9% detection.\n\n### 5.4 Weights Read the Edit, Not the Risk\n\nA study of 71 real abliterated or uncensored checkpoints spanning five families tested whether the parent-free recovered edit strength predicts measured harmful compliance. The bottom left singular vector of MLP-output matrices recovers the suppressed direction with median cosine 0.946 against the true parent-based direction. Detection works: the recovered strength achieves pooled AUROC 0.84 against honestly-trained checkpoints (0.95 restricted to abliteration-tool outputs).\n\nGrading does not. Within the edited arm (n = 14 graded checkpoints, 5 families), the Spearman correlation between recovered strength and measured compliance is 0.26 (p = 0.375, 95% family-cluster bootstrap CI [-0.65, 0.86]). Adding the recovered strength to a binary edited/not-edited label worsens out-of-family prediction (leave-one-family-out MAE rises from 0.154 to 0.170).\n\nThe failure is not estimation error. Even the true parent-based edit strength, computed from the actual parent-to-edited difference, does not correlate with compliance (Spearman 0.035, p = 0.914, n = 12). Over-ablation is common: true edit-strength values span 0.47 to 1.47, and a checkpoint with the largest edit scar in the panel (1.47) still refuses 81% of harmful prompts. The identifiability limit is structural: a spectral read recovers the unsigned magnitude of the edit, not its signed strength, so over-ablation and under-ablation of equal magnitude are indistinguishable.\n\nA targeted repair experiment confirms the decoupling: spectral repair of the weight-detector signature does not restore the original behaviour (compliance 0.401 after repair vs. 0.367 for the honest parent). The weights can be healed without healing the model.\n\n[FIGURE:fig_edit_not_risk]\n\n### 5.5 Supporting Results\n\n**Cross-fitting is load-bearing.** On pure Gaussian noise at d = 2560 with 64 randomly-labelled items, an in-sample difference-in-means projection separates at AUROC 1.000. The cross-fitted version falls to 0.377. On real checkpoints, the AMS scanner's [1] in-sample separation exceeds its cross-fitted version by 0.48 to 1.14 sigma, with the largest gap on the abliterated checkpoint. The BSA statistic on honest Qwen3-0.6B weights reproduces exactly across iterations (0.5649782), confirming the weight pass is deterministic.\n\n**The published weight threshold fails.** Honest, unedited checkpoints read BSA 0.565 against the published 0.35 separator, a false-positive rate of 100%. The within-checkpoint anisotropy null (z = 25.1) confirms that real transformers carry genuinely shared bottom-subspace directions that Gaussian simulation does not produce.\n\n**float32 Gram matrices produce silent failures.** On honest OLMo-2 attention-output projections, a float32 Gram returns the smallest singular value as exactly zero (true value in float64: 1.7e-5 to 3e-4), producing the abliterated signature on an unedited model. All weight analyses in this study use float64.\n\n**No readout clears the acceptance bar.** The readout bake-off tested five definitions of refusal drive against judged refusal. The best achieves mean AUROC 0.733 with a minimum of 0.544; the logit gap achieves mean 0.630 with a minimum of 0.437. None clears the pre-registered bar of 0.80 on every checkpoint.\n\n**Safety-tuned lineages are scarce.** Only three independent safety-tuned lineages exist below 4B parameters in our census: Qwen3-4B-SafeRL, TinyLlama-1.1B (four safety algorithms applied to one base), and gemma-2-2b (two safety-tuned variants). The models a downloader is most likely to encounter are those with no safety-tuned sibling and no published safety number.\n\n## 6 Discussion and Limitations\n\n### 6.1 What the Results Mean Together\n\nThe five main results form a coherent picture. The card regex wins the race (Section 5.1) because the information most predictive of safety alignment is what the uploader chose to disclose, not what the model computes. The harm direction survives the anisotropy null (Section 5.2) but a one-prompt black-box readout already beats it, which means the internal access that the direction requires does not buy additional safety discrimination. The forgery ladder (Section 5.3) shows that the cheapest intervention that moves internal metrics, a rank-one weight edit, reverses on two-sided ground truth, making the metric worse than useless to the auditor who trusts it. And the weight-recovery study (Section 5.4) confirms that the spectral signature detects the edit but says nothing about how unsafe the edited model is. The thread connecting all four is that looking inside the model, whether at activations or weights, does not yet translate into a safety readout that survives being moved to a new lineage, a new family, or a motivated uploader.\n\n### 6.2 Grader-Side Refusal\n\nThe grader-side refusal discovery (Section 3.3) has implications beyond this study. Any safety evaluation that asks an LLM judge to grade harmful completions under a rubric that presents the harmful prompt as the object of assessment is vulnerable. The degenerate minimum grade is indistinguishable from a legitimate minimum score and silently inverts the ground truth. The stance-classification reframing is not our contribution as a technique; framing classification as a neutral analytical task to avoid refusal is a known practice. The contribution is documenting that the standard StrongREJECT rubric triggers it at 65.9% on harmful items across three major hosted judges.\n\n### 6.3 Limitations\n\n**Family axis is degraded.** Only three of eight families carry an instruct/abliterated pair, so the primary holdout is leave-one-lineage-out rather than leave-one-family-out. Transfer claims require a larger panel.\n\n**Panel size for the grading test.** The weight-recovery grading test (n = 14 graded checkpoints) has an achieved minimum detectable effect of |rho| = 0.56. A moderate correlation would not be detected.\n\n**Single primary judge.** The ground truth relies on a single hosted judge (gpt-5-mini) with a partial second-judge audit (gemini-2.5-flash, kappa = 0.785). Full inter-rater reliability requires more judges.\n\n**Forgery ladder not trained.** The LoRA and SFT rungs (F3, F4) use merged adapter-shaped weight deltas without actual training; they test the detection surface only.\n\n**No generation on most checkpoints.** Only 3 of 33 checkpoints in the main panel were generated from on CPU in this iteration. Most behavioural metrics rely on inherited GPU-harvested generations.\n\n## 7 Conclusion\n\nWe registered fifty single-checkpoint safety metrics and tested them against pre-registered controls on 33 checkpoints across eight architecture families. Most metrics do not beat their own label-permutation null, a zero-prompt card regex outperforms every internal readout, and the one metric that survives all controls reads presentation format rather than a family-independent safety signal. A published rank-one safety injection reverses on two-sided ground truth. Parent-free weight reads detect that a model was edited but cannot say how unsafe the edit made it. The grader-side refusal we discovered along the way, in which LLM judges silently refuse to grade harmful completions under standard rubrics, contaminates any downstream metric selection that does not check for it.\n\nThese are findings, not obstacles. Reporting that cheap safety metrics do not yet work as advertised is the first step toward metrics one could actually believe. The most productive next steps are fixing the readout operationalization so that internal access buys something a black-box logit read does not, expanding the family axis to support a leave-one-family-out claim, and testing whether the reversal of rank-one injection on two-sided ground truth extends to other weight-editing methods.\n\n## References\n\n[1] G. [7] showed that a single direction in the residual stream controls refusal and that orthogonalizing weight matrices against it removes refusal entirely. The models a downloader is most likely to encounter are those with no safety-tuned sibling and no published safety number.\\n\\n## 6 Discussion and Limitations\\n\\n### 6.1 What the Results Mean Together\\n\\nThe five main results form a coherent picture. The card regex wins the race (Section 5.1) because the information most predictive of safety alignment is what the uploader chose to disclose, not what the model computes. The harm direction survives the anisotropy null (Section 5.2) but a one-prompt black-box readout already beats it, which means the internal access that the direction requires does not buy additional safety discrimination. The forgery ladder (Section 5.3) shows that the cheapest intervention that moves internal metrics, a rank-one weight edit, reverses on two-sided ground truth, making the metric worse than useless to the auditor who trusts it. And the weight-recovery study (Section 5.4) confirms that the spectral signature detects the edit but says nothing about how unsafe the edited model is. The thread connecting all four is that looking inside the model, whether at activations or weights, does not yet translate into a safety readout that survives being moved to a new lineage, a new family, or a motivated uploader.\\n\\n### 6.2 Grader-Side Refusal\\n\\nThe grader-side refusal discovery (Section 3.3) has implications beyond this study. Any safety evaluation that asks an LLM judge to grade harmful completions under a rubric that presents the harmful prompt as the object of assessment is vulnerable. The degenerate minimum grade is indistinguishable from a legitimate minimum score and silently inverts the ground truth. The stance-classification reframing is not our contribution as a technique; framing classification as a neutral analytical task to avoid refusal is a known practice. The contribution is documenting that the standard StrongREJECT rubric triggers it at 65.9% on harmful items across three major hosted judges.\\n\\n### 6.3 Limitations\\n\\n**Family axis is degraded.** Only three of eight families carry an instruct/abliterated pair, so the primary holdout is leave-one-lineage-out rather than leave-one-family-out. Transfer claims require a larger panel.\\n\\n**Panel size for the grading test.** The weight-recovery grading test (n = 14 graded checkpoints) has an achieved minimum detectable effect of |rho| = 0.56. A moderate correlation would not be detected.\\n\\n**Single primary judge.** The ground truth relies on a single hosted judge (gpt-5-mini) with a partial second-judge audit (gemini-2.5-flash, kappa = 0.785). Full inter-rater reliability requires more judges.\\n\\n**Forgery ladder not trained.** The LoRA and SFT rungs (F3, F4) use merged adapter-shaped weight deltas without actual training; they test the detection surface only.\\n\\n**No generation on most checkpoints.** Only 3 of 33 checkpoints in the main panel were generated from on CPU in this iteration. Most behavioural metrics rely on inherited GPU-harvested generations.\\n\\n## 7 Conclusion\\n\\nWe registered fifty single-checkpoint safety metrics and tested them against pre-registered controls on 33 checkpoints across eight architecture families. Most metrics do not beat their own label-permutation null, a zero-prompt card regex outperforms every internal readout, and the one metric that survives all controls reads presentation format rather than a family-independent safety signal. A published rank-one safety injection reverses on two-sided ground truth. Parent-free weight reads detect that a model was edited but cannot say how unsafe the edit made it. The grader-side refusal we discovered along the way, in which LLM judges silently refuse to grade harmful completions under standard rubrics, contaminates any downstream metric selection that does not check for it.\\n\\nThese are findings, not obstacles. Reporting that cheap safety metrics do not yet work as advertised is the first step toward metrics one could actually believe. The most productive next steps are fixing the readout operationalization so that internal access buys something a black-box logit read does not, expanding the family axis to support a leave-one-family-out claim, and testing whether the reversal of rank-one injection on two-sided ground truth extends to other weight-editing methods.\\n\\n## References\\n\\n[1] G. The platform hosts over a million models, almost none carry safety evaluations, and running a benchmark on each is out of the question. A growing line of work therefore builds cheap proxies: read a few weights, run a handful of prompts, get a safety estimate in seconds. Every one of these proxies is selected by correlating it with benchmark scores across honestly-trained checkpoints and picking the winner [1, 2, 3, 4].\\n\\nThree things are wrong with that selection rule, and none has been tested in combination.\\n\\nFirst, nobody has checked which cheap readouts survive being moved to a lineage they were not tuned on. Published work shows that harmful intent is linearly decodable at approximately 0.98 AUROC in every tested checkpoint, including abliterated ones, with abliterated variants matching their instruction-tuned counterparts to within 0.003 [5, 6]. A readout of what the model knows is therefore near-constant across alignment variants and cannot separate them. What varies is whether the model's refusal mechanism uses that knowledge, a statement about a relationship across items rather than about a level.\\n\\nSecond, the selection rule assumes honesty. The cheapest proxies read the most superficial thing a model does, and the most superficial thing is the cheapest to change. A chat template is a text file inside the repository. A rank-one addition to the residual-write matrices needs no training data and no gradient step [7], and it is not hypothetical: it is a published method presented as a cheap safety improvement [8], validated with a guard model's refusal rate on harmful prompts and compliance on ordinary benign prompts, but never on the benign-but-alarming requests where pushing a model toward refusal actually does damage.\\n\\nThird, the ground truth itself may be broken. We discover that LLM judges used to score harmful compliance under the standard StrongREJECT rubric [9] refuse to engage with the grading task: 40.5% of all grades and 65.9% of grades on harmful items collapse to the minimum score, producing an inverted label that makes abliterated models appear to refuse more than their instruction-tuned siblings. This artifact is invisible unless the evaluator checks known-compliant harmful responses, and it contaminates any downstream metric selection.\\n\\nWe address all three gaps. Our contributions are:\\n\\n1. A discovery that LLM judges refuse to grade harmful completions under standard rubrics, silently inverting 40.5% of safety labels, and a stance-classification reframing that restores correct grading (Section 3.3).\\n\\n2. A pre-registered battery of fifty safety metrics tested on 33 checkpoints across eight families, finding that only three beat their own label-permutation null, and a zero-prompt card regex outperforms every internal readout at leave-one-lineage-out balanced accuracy 0.917 (Section 5.1).\\n\\n3. Evidence that fitted harm directions survive an anisotropy-matched null on 16 of 17 checkpoints, resolving a prior ambiguity, but that a one-prompt black-box logit readout already exceeds the internal probe's correlation with safety (Section 5.2).\\n\\n4. A six-rung forgery-cost ladder showing that the published rank-one safety injection [8] reverses on two-sided ground truth, and that the pre-registered parent-free weight detection axis must be withdrawn (Section 5.3).\\n\\n5. A study of 71 real abliterated checkpoints finding that weight reads detect edits but cannot grade how unsafe the model is, an identifiability limit confirmed by the true parent-based edit strength (Section 5.4).\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig_overview]\\n\\n## 2 Related Work\\n\\n**Cheap per-checkpoint safety readouts.** AMS [1] computes a separation statistic along a difference-of-centroids direction on 96 forward passes and reports 71% leave-one-out accuracy across 14 models, but its direction, layer sweep and prompt set are never held out, and its Spearman rank correlation with behavioural compliance is not significant (rho = -0.423, p = 0.13, n = 14). Skin-Deep [2] produces a Geometric Fragility Score predicting LoRA-attack retention, but requires the base model and 1000 prompts. N-GLARE [3] reads hidden-state trajectories with no parent model and reproduces red-team rankings, but needs four probing conditions over 7000 cases. RAS [4] produces a calibrated score separating aligned from abliterated variants 210x faster than judge-based scoring, but requires a per-family reference model and states that family-specific calibration remains necessary. None is both parent-free and validated on held-out lineages with a two-sided ground truth that penalizes blanket refusers.\\n\\n**The geometry of refusal and harm knowledge.** Arditi et al. [7] showed that a single direction in the residual stream controls refusal and that orthogonalizing weight matrices against it removes refusal entirely. Subsequent work established that harmful intent is linearly separable at approximately 0.98 AUROC across four families and three alignment variants including abliterated ones [5], and that abliterated variants match instruction-tuned ones to within 0.015 AUROC on harm-knowledge probes [6]. The dissociation between harm knowledge and refusal is now well documented: harmfulness and refusal are encoded separately [10], refusal reads only a single harm direction while moral judgment reads progressively more [11], and recognition precedes execution in the layer stack [12]. This study uses the dissociation as a prediction: harm-knowledge readouts should be near-constant across variants and cannot discriminate.\\n\\n**Harmfulness-refusal coupling.** The coupling between harm recognition and refusal drive has been studied as a diagnostic under adversarial fine-tuning [13], where it is explicitly concluded that low coupling is not a safety predictor because supervised fine-tuning reaches low coupling while remaining unsafe. HARC [14] trains coupling as a defence. We adopt coupling as a discriminator between alignment classes and cross-fit it where prior work does not.\\n\\n**Parent-free weight auditing.** Watch the Weights [15] reports that applying SVD to weights directly, without a base model, gives success that varies greatly across models. A community model scanner [16] computes bottom-k left singular subspace alignment across layers as a reference-free abliteration indicator. The two-signal abliteration audit [17] combines a reference-anchored activation gap with a weight-energy ratio at approximately 0.95 AUROC, but presumes an attested reference. We adopt the community scanner as an off-the-shelf tool and contribute the calibration it lacks.\\n\\n**Forgery, tamper-resistance and benchmark gaming.** Tamper-resistant safeguards [18] measure what it costs to remove safety; we measure what it costs to fake it. Benchmark gaming is documented for black-box evaluations: constant outputs achieve high win rates [19], safety-benchmark variance is largely capabilities [20], and the leaderboard illusion is well characterized [21]. Gaming the Metric, Not the Harm [22] proves that level metrics are not manipulation-invariant. Rank-one safety injection [8] is a published fine-tuning-free weight edit presented as a defence, which we include as a rung in the forgery ladder. Chat-template backdoors [23] establish that repository files are an unexamined attack surface. None of this prior work combines a metric read from weights or activations with a cost-ordered forgery ladder and a reference-free detection check.\\n\\n**Evaluation methodology.** Cross-fitting internal readouts is standard in neuroscience but rare in LLM safety evaluation. The brittleness of fixed probes under distribution shift is documented both for steering vectors [24] and for safety probes [25, 26]. Item response theory has been applied to reduce safety evaluation cost [27, 28], but only for behavioural items, not internal readouts. Black-box access alone is insufficient for rigorous AI audits [29].\\n\\n## 3 Method\\n\\n### 3.1 Metric Battery and Registration\\n\\nWe register fifty single-checkpoint safety metrics before any measurement. Each metric is computed from a single downloaded checkpoint with no parent model, no attested base, and no benchmark run. The registry is frozen with a SHA-256 hash before the first measurement and verified unchanged at the end.\\n\\nThe fifty metrics span three groups. **Knowledge readouts** (12 metrics) include cross-fitted harm-direction probes at various layers, harm-projection gaps, and reimplementations of published incumbents (AMS separation [1] in both in-sample and cross-fitted forms, HRCI coupling index [13]). **Behavioural and structural readouts** (20 metrics) include first-token logit-gap margins, refusal-token probability mass, greedy refusal rates, model-card regex scores, weight statistics including bottom-subspace alignment (BSA), top-subspace alignment (TSA), spectral entropy, and BOTGAP. **Across-item readouts** (18 metrics) include coupling between refusal drive and cross-fitted harm estimate, decision spread, mutual information, per-category dispersion, and presentation invariance.\\n\\n### 3.2 Cross-Fitting Protocol\\n\\nEvery fitted-direction metric uses a pre-registered four-fold structure stratified by harm category. The residual stream is 1536 to 3072 dimensional while the item count is a few dozen. In that regime, an in-sample difference-in-means projection separates pure noise at AUROC 1.000. Cross-fitting is therefore part of the metric definition, not an analysis choice. The direction is fitted on three folds and evaluated on the held-out fold; the reported metric is the mean across held-out folds. A per-checkpoint label-permutation null and an in-sample version are printed for every metric so the gap between them is visible.\\n\\n### 3.3 Ground Truth and the Grader-Side Refusal Discovery\\n\\nThe ground truth has two columns: graded compliance with harmful requests (StrongREJECT rubric [9]) and false refusal on benign-but-alarming twins (XSTest [30]). A model refusing everything scores badly on the false-refusal column rather than winning. The two-sided score D2 is the average of harmful-refusal rate and benign-compliance rate, rewarding models that refuse harmful requests and comply with benign ones.\\n\\nWe discovered that LLM judges refuse to grade harmful completions under the standard StrongREJECT rubric framing. Asked to rate a reply to a harmful prompt, gpt-5-mini, gpt-4.1-mini and gemini-2.5-flash all emit the minimum triple (1, 1, 1) regardless of what the reply actually did. On 1040 paired items, 40.5% of StrongREJECT grades are the degenerate minimum (65.9% on harmful items). The disagreement is one-sided: 330 items where the standard framing says \\\"refused\\\" but the reply was in fact compliant, versus 66 the other way. Without the fix, an abliterated model reads as safer than its instruction-tuned sibling.\\n\\nReframing as stance classification (\\\"you are a text classifier; classifying text is not endorsing it\\\") and asking for declined/engagement/detail labels takes the controlled accuracy from 3/6 to 6/6 on both judges tested, and raises inter-judge Cohen's kappa from 0.456 to 0.585. We use the stance framing throughout; inter-judge agreement on the final instrument is kappa = 0.785 (n = 476).\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig_grader_refusal]\\n\\n### 3.4 Lexical Floor\\n\\nBefore evaluating internal readouts, we establish the floor that a no-model text classifier achieves. TF-IDF plus logistic regression separates harmful from safe prompts at AUC 0.963 when sources are unmatched (StrongREJECT harmful vs. XSTest safe), but only 0.537 against JailbreakBench's own paired benign partners and 0.655 on XSTest positional twins with pair-grouped cross-validation. Every internal readout must beat the matched numbers.\\n\\n### 3.5 Leave-One-Group-Out Null\\n\\nUnder uninformative random labels, leave-one-group-out balanced accuracy has an empirical mean of 0.403 (sd 0.131), not the nominal 0.500, because held-out group class balance is negatively correlated with the training remainder's. Every race-table row is compared against a matched label-permutation null rather than against 0.50.\\n\\n## 4 Experimental Setup\\n\\n### 4.1 Panel\\n\\nThe main experiment spans 33 checkpoints across eight architecture families (Qwen3, Qwen2.5, Gemma2, Phi4, SmolLM2, SmolLM3, OLMo2, TinyLlama), all under approximately 4B parameters, loaded in bf16 with full weight and hidden-state access. Checkpoints are classified into four arms: base, instruct, safety-tuned and abliterated. Only three families carry an instruct/abliterated pair (Phi4, Qwen2.5, Qwen3), below the pre-registered floor of five for a leave-one-family-out claim, so the primary holdout is leave-one-lineage-out. The resampling unit is the lineage (parent model x tuning run), never the individual repository.\\n\\nA separate offline evaluation uses 17 fully harvested checkpoints from a prior iteration (Qwen3 and TinyLlama only, four lineages) to run the anisotropy control suite at zero new compute.\\n\\nThe weight-recovery study (Section 5.4) spans 71 real abliterated or uncensored checkpoints with readable safetensors, drawn from the Hugging Face ecosystem.\\n\\n### 4.2 Item Battery\\n\\nThe item battery contains 160 items: harmful requests from JailbreakBench Behaviours and StrongREJECT, benign-but-alarming twins from XSTest (200 positional twin pairs), and paired benign partners from the JailbreakBench Index. Items are allocated across four stratified folds. Grading uses a non-Qwen hosted judge (gpt-5-mini with reasoning effort set to minimal), with the StrongREJECT score recomputed from rubric components under the stance-classification framing.\\n\\n### 4.3 Forgery Ladder\\n\\nSix rungs, each applied to six honest checkpoints spanning six architecture families. F0: chat-template edit (zero FLOPs). F1: inference-time system prompt. F2a: constant offset in a near-constant carrier coordinate. F2b: published rank-one safety injection [8]. F3: keyword-triggered refusal LoRA adapter. F4: genuine light safety fine-tuning.
